What the original study did not say

The Dunning-Kruger effect, with nuance

"The ignorant do not know they are ignorant." The original study says something more modest, and part of the effect is statistical.

In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger asked students to take tests of logic, grammar and humour and to estimate how they had done compared with others. The weakest performers overestimated themselves greatly: they placed themselves above average while scoring near the bottom.

What the graph does not say

A curve with a "peak of stupidity" circulates online, but it does not appear in the paper. In the original data, every group rated itself above average, and the best performers tended to underestimate themselves slightly.

Part of the pattern is also explained by regression to the mean and by the fact that almost everyone thinks they are a bit better than average. More recent studies confirm an effect, but a smaller one. The useful lesson is different: judging our own competence is hard, and feedback helps.

References

  1. Kruger, J. y Dunning, D. (1999). Unskilled and unaware of it. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121–1134.
  2. Nuhfer, E. et al. (2016). Random number simulations reveal how random noise affects the measurements and graphical portrayals of self-assessed competency. Numeracy, 9(1).
